profiles.meeting_scenario: A staff engineer and a senior applied ML product engineer at a developer-tools company are holding a brainstorming meeting about a new recommendation feature for their IDE plugin, drawing on lessons from the CROSSMINER experience with OSS-based software-engineering recommenders. Their team wants to identify 2-3 candidate features that suggest relevant OSS artifacts such as API usage examples, third-party libraries, or documentation while developers work on real tasks. The agenda is to generate ideas, lightly screen them for near-term prototyping potential, and agree on what an initial internal check would look like before presenting the concept to the wider platform team. The expected outcome is a shortlist of promising recommendation concepts plus a shared-sounding but still implicit understanding of how to keep the effort 'using what we already have,' make it useful 'in context,' test it 'on internal projects,' and ensure it improves the 'current search experience.'

members.name: Nina Park
members.role: Staff Software Engineer, Developer Intelligence Platform
members.expertise: IDE telemetry pipelines, code search infrastructure, repository indexing, offline experimentation
members.background: Nina has spent eight years building backend systems for developer tools and previously led integration work for code navigation and API-usage mining features in a large enterprise IDE.
members.private_state: She wants the brainstorm to land on ideas her team can prototype mostly with existing plugin events, backend indexes, and ranking infrastructure, because she has little spare implementation capacity and wants to avoid privacy review or plugin-surface changes.
hidden_assumptions: If they say they should build it 'using what we already have,' that means no new client-side collection points and no new visible IDE touchpoints beyond existing plugin surfaces.
When someone says a recommender should work 'in context,' the obvious context is the active repository and coding session: file, imports, call graph neighborhood, and dependency graph.
Testing an idea 'on internal projects' naturally means replaying or scoring it against logs and indexed snapshots from company repositories rather than interrupting engineers for live trials.
Improving the 'current search experience' means the recommendation layer should make the existing search/ranking stack retrieve better artifacts or rank them earlier for the same developer intent.

members.name: Leo Martins
members.expertise: recommender systems, developer workflow UX, internal dogfooding, API/documentation ranking
members.background: Leo joined from a startup that built contextual knowledge assistants for engineers and has been focusing on how recommendation features become visible and useful in day-to-day development workflows.
members.private_state: He wants the meeting to produce something compelling enough for a roadmap demo, and he is comfortable assuming a narrow temporary UI flow or lightweight instrumentation later if that is what makes the value legible to users.
hidden_assumptions: If they say they should build it 'using what we already have,' that still allows assembling a quick experimental touchpoint from existing UI frameworks and plugin extension hooks, as long as they are not inventing a whole new platform.

When someone says a recommender should work 'in context,' that naturally includes task-level signals around the repo such as issue text, recent pull requests, onboarding flows, and dependency intent before coding starts.
Testing an idea 'on internal projects' naturally means having a few internal developers use it on real company codebases or seeded tasks, even if the trial is informal and brief.
Improving the 'current search experience' means lowering the effort and time it takes developers to find something useful in their workflow, even if the underlying search backend is unchanged.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'using what we already have' permits
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to keep the prototype practical by building it 'using what we already have.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the idea must fit inside current telemetry schemas, current backend indexes, and current visible plugin surfaces, with no new collection or new user-facing entry point.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the idea can still include a thin experimental UI or lightweight hook assembled from existing plugin frameworks and components, because that still counts as reusing what the team already has.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like ordinary feasibility shorthand and both interpretations are plausibly conservative, so each hears the other as agreeing to a low-risk prototype without noticing they draw the implementation boundary in different places.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They repeatedly discuss surfacing recommendations 'in context' for the developer.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 takes 'in context' to mean signals available from the active coding session and repository state, such as the current file, imports, dependency graph, and nearby API calls.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 takes 'in context' to include broader task framing around the repository, such as issue descriptions, onboarding/setup moments, recent PR discussions, and other cues about what the developer is trying to do.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are standard uses of the phrase in developer-tooling conversations, and because they trade examples rather than explicitly stating system boundaries, the narrower and broader scopes feel compatible instead of contradictory.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to test ideas 'on internal projects'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that shortlisted ideas should be tested 'on internal projects' before a broader review.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means running offline ranking and acceptance analyses over logs, indexed code snapshots, or reconstructed tasks from the company's internal repositories.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means giving a few internal engineers access to the feature on real company projects and collecting lightweight feedback from short dogfooding sessions.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both approaches genuinely involve internal codebases and are commonly described as testing on internal projects, so the wording creates a natural illusion of alignment even though one plan is offline and the other requires live usage.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to improve the 'current search experience'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They say any recommendation idea should improve the 'current search experience.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 treats this as improving the quality of what the search/retrieval stack returns for the same underlying need, for example by making relevant APIs, docs, or libraries rank earlier or appear with less query reformulation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 treats this as reducing the developer's time-to-find or search detours in the workflow, even if the recommendation is delivered through a sidebar, proactive panel, or other assistance outside the classic search results flow.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase is deliberately broad and product-positive, and both criteria are reasonable ways to describe better search from their respective backgrounds, so neither person feels a need to unpack whether 'experience' refers to ranking quality or workflow effort.

turns.inner_thought: I need this to end with ideas my team can actually prototype from the assets we already run: plugin telemetry that's already collected, backend indexes, repository graphs, and ranking infrastructure. If this turns into new client instrumentation, a new visible surface, or anything that triggers privacy review, it will stall immediately. CROSSMINER is useful as inspiration, but only the parts we can map onto existing search and indexing systems.
turns.utterance: Thanks for jumping on. I’d like us to leave with two or three OSS-based recommendation ideas for the IDE plugin that take the useful lessons from CROSSMINER but stay practical for a near-term prototype. If we can keep it grounded in things we can build using what we already have, then agree on a simple first check before taking it to the wider platform team, that would be ideal.

turns.inner_thought: Practical is good, but I want something that feels meaningful in the workflow, not just a clever backend ranking tweak. The strongest opportunities are where recommendations show up around a concrete need: unfamiliar dependencies, figuring out what direction to take, or trying to orient around a task. To me, 'in context' includes the broader project intent around the code, not just what's already typed in the editor.
turns.utterance: Yeah, that tracks. My instinct would be to focus on the moments where recommendations can help developers in context, especially when they’re trying to make sense of something unfamiliar and need a better path to the right dependency, example, or documentation.

turns.inner_thought: A good anchor is an editor-time recommender driven by active repo and coding-session signals: current file, imports, nearby API calls, dependency graph, similar repositories. That stays inside our current plugin events and backend retrieval systems. If I phrase it broadly, Leo will hear the same thing and we can keep moving.
turns.utterance: One concrete direction could be an editor-time recommender that surfaces API usage examples, and maybe related libraries, from similar repositories while someone is coding. That feels aligned with helping in context, and it’s the kind of thing we could plausibly assemble using what we already have.

turns.inner_thought: I want to stretch that idea earlier in the workflow, before much code exists. Recommendations can be useful when the developer is still forming intent, getting oriented, or deciding what path to take. I should keep it broad and say 'broader project intent' so Nina hears it as compatible rather than as a request for specific new signals.
turns.utterance: I like that. I’d just broaden the same theme a bit: recommendations in context could also help before much code is written, when someone is still orienting around a task and broader project intent could cue the right docs or dependency suggestions early.

turns.inner_thought: I should reinforce the implementation boundary without sounding like I'm shutting ideas down. Existing indexes, existing events, existing plugin capabilities—that's the fence. If we stay there, this can be real; if not, it turns into platform work my team can't absorb.
turns.utterance: That seems reasonable. As we narrow, I’d still put extra weight on options we can assemble quickly from our existing indexes, events, and plugin capabilities, just so we stay inside using what we already have and don’t turn the brainstorm into a platform project.

turns.inner_thought: I agree on lightweight, but I want to preserve room for a thin experimental touchpoint if that's what makes the value legible. Reusing existing plugin frameworks and extension hooks still counts as using what we already have to me. I won't say panel or entry point directly; better to frame it as making the recommendation visible enough to evaluate.
turns.utterance: Totally. I’m not looking for anything heavy either. I just want to leave enough room that, if needed, we can make the recommendation visible enough to evaluate while still staying within using what we already have. Otherwise it can be hard to tell whether it’s actually improving the current search experience.

turns.inner_thought: For me the right screen is whether this makes our existing search and retrieval stack bring better artifacts forward for the same need. Available project signals should help rank APIs, examples, docs, or libraries earlier, with less query reformulation. That's measurable with what we already log.
turns.utterance: Right. I think we should prioritize ideas that clearly improve the current search experience, especially where available project signals help us surface the right artifacts earlier instead of making people dig or reformulate what they’re already trying to find.

turns.inner_thought: I hear 'search experience' more broadly: less bouncing among code, docs, and search, faster time-to-useful-result, fewer detours in the workflow. It doesn't have to be a pure ranking win as long as the developer gets to something helpful faster. I'll phrase it in workflow terms without making the delivery mechanism explicit.
turns.utterance: Agreed. The bar for me is basically whether it reduces how much wandering around developers do before they land on something useful. If it shortens that back-and-forth between search, docs, and code, that’s a real improvement to the current search experience.

turns.inner_thought: Before this grows legs, I want the validation plan to mean offline passes over internal repositories, interaction traces, and indexed snapshots. That's the fastest, safest way to test on internal projects and gives us enough signal for a first review without any coordination burden.
turns.utterance: Makes sense. For validation, I’d say whichever ideas survive this pass should be tested on internal projects first. We can do a fast initial check there before we ask for a broader review.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, and I really want at least a little real-use signal, even if it's informal. Seeing how the recommendations perform against real internal workflows would tell us whether the timing and usefulness are obvious to people. I'll keep it abstract enough that Nina won't hear it as a request for a separate trial setup.
turns.utterance: Yep, testing on internal projects first feels like the right bar. And if we can, I’d love to include some signal about how it performs against real internal workflows, just so we know the recommendations are actually useful in practice.

turns.inner_thought: We can keep the shortlist broad at the surface. In my head, the first item is clearly session-and-repo-based example recommendation. The second can sound like broader project-context suggestions, but I still intend it to be served from project artifacts and repository state we already index. That wording should keep us aligned enough to move forward.
turns.utterance: So maybe the shortlist is: first, editor-time API or usage-example recommendations; second, broader project-context suggestions for libraries or documentation tied to what the developer is working on. Both seem connected to improving the current search experience without getting too diffuse.

turns.inner_thought: Good, that's enough to turn into a roadmap-friendly concept note. I'll frame both candidates as practical and keep the testing plan lightweight. In my mind that still leaves room for a small visible flow and some real internal usage signal, but I don't need to unpack that here because 'using what we already have' and 'on internal projects' sounds like we're aligned.
turns.utterance: I’m good with that. I’ll sketch up the two candidate concepts and a lightweight plan to test them on internal projects before the wider team review. I’ll keep it framed around using what we already have so it lands as a realistic next step.
